column2: The first prefatory discussion: that human social organization is necessary

The philosophers express this by saying, “Man is civic by nature,” that is, he cannot do without social organization, which in their terminology is the “city” (madīna), and which is the meaning of civilization (ʿumrān). The explanation is that God, glory be to Him, created man and constituted him in a form whose life and survival are sound only with food, and He guided him to seek it by his innate disposition and by the power to obtain it that He built into him. But the power of a single human being falls short of obtaining what he needs of that food, and does not supply him with the substance of his life from it. Even if we supposed the least that can be supposed of it, which is a day’s sustenance of wheat, say, it is obtained only through much processing: grinding, kneading and cooking. Each of these three operations needs vessels and tools that are completed only through a number of crafts, those of the blacksmith, the carpenter and the potter. And grant that he eats it as grain without processing: even so, to obtain it as grain he needs other labors, more than these: the sowing, the harvest and the threshing, which brings the grain out of the husk of the ear; and each of these needs the sowing, the harvest and the threshing that brings the grain out of the husk of the ear; and each of these needs a number of tools and many crafts, far more than the first. And it is impossible for the power of one man to suffice for all of that or for any part of it,

so the powers of many of his own kind must be joined together, so that sustenance is obtained for him and for them. Through cooperation, then, the amount sufficient for the need is obtained for many times their number. In the same way, each of them also needs, to defend himself, the help of his own kind. For when God, glory be to Him, set the natures in all the animals and apportioned the powers among them, He made the share of power of many of the speechless animals more complete than the share of man. The power of the horse, for example, is far greater than the power of man, and so is the power of the donkey and the bull, and the power of the lion and the elephant is many times his. And since aggression is natural in animals, He gave each of them a limb assigned to repelling whatever attack of another reaches it, and in place of all that He gave man thought and the hand. The hand is equipped for the crafts, in the service of thought, and the crafts provide him with the tools that take the place, for him, of the limbs prepared in all the other animals for defense: spears, for example, which take the place of butting horns; swords, which take the place of wounding claws; and shields, which take the place of hard skins; and so on, and other things besides, among those that Galen mentions in his book Manāfiʿ al-aʿḍāʾ (“On the Usefulness of the Parts”). So the power of one human being cannot withstand the power of one of the speechless animals, especially the predatory ones,

and he is unable, in sum, to defend himself against them alone, and his power does not suffice either to use the tools prepared for them. So in all of that cooperation with members of his own kind is indispensable. And unless this cooperation exists, he obtains no sustenance or food, and his life is not completed, because of the need for food in his life with which God the Exalted constituted him; nor does he obtain any defense of himself, for lack of weapons, so he becomes prey for the animals, destruction overtakes him before his life has run its course, and the human species comes to nothing. But when there is cooperation, he obtains sustenance for food and weapons for defense, and God’s wisdom is completed in his survival and in the preservation of his species. So this social organization is necessary for the human species; otherwise their existence would not be complete, nor would what God intended be fulfilled, that they inhabit and build up the world and that He make them His vicegerents. And this is the meaning of civilization, which we have made the subject of this science. In this discourse there is a kind of establishing of the subject within the art of which it is the subject. And although this is not obligatory for the master of an art, since it is established in the art of logic that the master of a science is not required to establish the subject within that science, it is also not among the things they forbid, so establishing it counts as a voluntary extra. And God is the one who grants success, by His favor.

Then, once this social organization has come about for human beings as we have set it out, and the civilization of the world is complete through them, there must be a restraining authority to keep them from one another, because of the aggression and injustice in their animal natures. The weapons that were provided to repel the aggression of the speechless animals from them are not sufficient to repel aggression among themselves, since they exist for all of them. So there must be something else to repel the aggression of some of them against others, and it cannot come from outside them, since all the animals fall short of their faculties of perception and their inspirations. So that restraining authority must be one of them, who has over them mastery, sovereignty and a dominating hand, so that no one reaches another with aggression. And this is the meaning of royal authority. It has become clear to you from this that man has a natural characteristic which they cannot do without. It is also found in some of the speechless animals, according to what the philosophers mention, as in bees and locusts, from what has been found by inductive observation in them of rule, submission and following of a leader from among their own individuals who is distinguished from them in his make and body. But that exists in creatures other than man by virtue of innate disposition and guidance, not by virtue of thought and statecraft: “He gave everything its created form, then guided it” (20: 50). And the philosophers add to this proof, in that they try to establish prophecy by rational evidence, and that it is a natural characteristic of man, so they carry this proof to a final point,

and that human beings must have the restraining rule. Then they say after that that this rule exists through a law decreed by God, brought by one of the human beings, and that he must be distinguished from them by the special properties of guidance that God places in him, so that submission to him and acceptance from him come about, until the rule is completed among them and over them without denial or rejection. This proposition of the philosophers is not demonstrative, as you can see, since existence and the life of human beings can be complete without it, through what the ruler imposes for himself or through the group solidarity (ʿaṣabiyya) by which he is able to overpower them and make them follow his path. For the People of the Book and the followers of the prophets are few in comparison with the Magians, who have no scripture, since they are the majority of the people of the world; and yet they have had dynasties and monuments, to say nothing of life. And they have them in this age as well, in the deviant zones in the north and south, in contrast to the life of human beings in chaos, without any restraining authority at all, which is impossible. By this their error becomes clear to you regarding the necessity of prophecies, and that it is not a rational matter: it is perceived only through the revealed law (sharʿ), as is the doctrine of the early generations (salaf) of the community. And God is the guardian of success and guidance.
